draft.title: Answering an unseen text question
card: An unseen text is an extract you have not studied before. Short-answer questions usually ask how a technique shows an experience, such as loneliness or hope.
Underline the technique or the experience it names. This tells you what to look for before you read the extract.
Choose one or two clear examples that match the question. Quote only a few words, then name the technique.
In a few sentences, say how the technique shows the experience and what the reader feels or understands. Naming a technique without its effect earns little.
draft.remember: Question first, then one or two clear examples, then the effect on the reader.

a.q: Why should a student read the question before reading an unseen extract?
opts: It shows what to look for as they read
It lets them skip the extract and still answer
It means they only need to name techniques
It lets them use the same answer for any extract
a.why: The question names the technique or experience to focus on, so the student can spot useful examples while reading. Naming techniques alone is not enough, because the answer must also explain the effect.
a.clue: Think about what the question tells you in advance.

b.q: An extract describes a boy waiting for exam results. The question asks how imagery shows his anxiety. Which response best answers it?
opts: The image of a stone in his gut makes his dread feel heavy
The writer uses imagery, a technique that appears often
The extract is about a boy waiting for his exam results
The writer uses short sentences and a few long ones too
b.why: It gives one clear example of imagery and explains what it shows about the anxiety. The option that only names imagery gives no example or effect. The option about sentence length does not address the imagery the question asks about.
b.clue: A strong answer has an example and an effect.

a.best: It shows what to look for as they read

b.best: The image of a stone in his gut makes his dread feel heavy
